doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Staying open to new music as one ages
summary: Roger Kellaway's Cello Quartet leads him to say he refuses to get stuck like many peers and welcomes world music and what young people do.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Roger had not been in L.A. very long. He had come out from New York when he did that and he had only been in L.A. a year or two when I first met him out here. I’d been aware of him from an early recording he’d made in New York, but yeah, that’s an interesting, and John Guerin is the drummer, the drummer I mentioned earlier, and Chuck Domenico. But again, for someone, I’m sixty years old, and particularly for people my age, both the players and the audience, usually I find in talking with them they have become pretty much stuck somewhere as far as what they consider good and bad and what they want to hear, what they don’t want to hear, what’s B.S. and what isn’t. And I don’t want that to

happen. I feel very strongly that that’s not — I don’t want that to be the way one ages. I think it’s much more important — I’m really fascinated with what young people are thinking and how they hear it and how they see it. And I think world music, for lack of a better category, is here definitely bigger than ever. I think Cuban music obviously is having a tremendous effect on what goes on here. I think in the next few years we’re going to see more and more of that influence. And so much of what goes on in the rock world, and in the classical world is so interesting that it’s a shame to miss it, I think. I mean I love everything that I grew up with, and have so much admiration for all of that, but I have the hardest time with people who say well I love Charlie Parker but I don’t understand what these kids are trying to do. And it’s exactly what people said about Charlie Parker in his day. It’s like they can’t see the irony that they are simply stuck the same way. And if Bird were alive I would hope that he would be trying to understand what some kid was doing. So anyway, that’s just a personal reflection in looking back.
Well it’s a good insight. And I think a good—
It’s hard to stay that way. As you get older inevitably you start to shut down. It’s just part of what happens I think. I think you need to fight it as long as you can.
I’ll have to remember that when I get home and my 15 year old turns on her music.
Yeah. I know. Well you know, not all of it’s good but there’s some interesting stuff going on and if you want to call it post modern, turn of the century attitude or whatever.
It’s pretty funny too because something she’s listening to now, the guy’s playing an old Wurlitzer electronic piano.
I know. Amazing, huh? And Farfisas.
Yeah. Hey, the classics will always be.
